reading.title: City Subway, Valley Bus
reading.purpose: Listen to two cousins compare their daily rides to school using precise comparison and contrast words.
paras: Sofia looked out the bus window as pines blurred past. "Your morning valley bus and my city subway resemble each other more than I expected," she told her cousin Eli. "Both run on strict timetables, and both carry half the neighborhood before eight o'clock."

"True," Eli said, shifting his backpack. "Our route manager is basically the small-town counterpart to your transit dispatcher—same job, different setting. Similarly, riders here memorize which seats stay warmest in January."

Sofia laughed. "We definitely differ on the scenery, though! You watch deer cross a creek while I stare at tiled tunnel walls." She tapped her watch. "Conversely, my train arrives every five minutes, whereas if you miss this bus, you wait nearly an hour."

"That part is rough," Eli admitted. "Still, people think rural transit is always empty. On the contrary, every bench fills up by the third stop. Likewise, our driver knows almost every student's name and waits ten seconds if someone is sprinting down the driveway."

"Our two commutes actually follow parallel patterns," Sofia said, "matching step for step from waking up early to checking the route app. Despite the noise and crowds underground, I kind of like the energy of my train."
Eli nodded as the school brick wall came into view. "Snowstorms slow my bus down sometimes. Nevertheless, I would not trade this window view for a tunnel. Both rides get us where we need to go."

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "counterpart" most nearly means
choices: a passenger who always sits near the warmest bus window
someone who fills the same role in a different place
a printed timetable posted inside a subway station
a driver who takes a slower path through the tall pines
qs.why: Eli explains that the route manager is the counterpart to a transit dispatcher: "same job, different setting."

qs.q: Which sentence shows the biggest difference in how often Sofia's train and Eli's bus arrive?
choices: Sofia looked out the bus window as pines blurred past.
Both run on strict timetables, and both carry half the neighborhood before eight o'clock.
"Conversely, my train arrives every five minutes, whereas if you miss this bus, you wait nearly an hour."
Snowstorms slow my bus down sometimes.
qs.why: This sentence contrasts the subway arriving every five minutes with the valley bus arriving nearly an hour later.

ev.text: "Conversely, my train arrives every five minutes, whereas if you miss this bus, you wait nearly an hour."

qs.q: Why does Eli say "On the contrary" when talking about rural transit?
choices: He wants to show that his bus is actually full, not empty.
He agrees with Sofia that the tiled subway walls look nicer.
He thinks the valley bus should stop running in January.
He wants to prove that city trains never get crowded at all.
qs.why: Eli corrects the common assumption that rural transit is empty by pointing out that every bench fills up by the third stop.

qs.q: What is this dialogue mostly about?
choices: Why city subway trains are faster and safer than mountain valley buses.
How a rural bus driver learns the names of every student on his route.
Why Sofia wishes she could move away from the noisy underground train.
How two different school commutes share surprising similarities.
qs.why: Sofia and Eli compare scenery, wait times, and habits, concluding that their commutes follow parallel patterns even though they differ.

clues.text: You watch deer cross a creek while I stare at tiled tunnel walls.
people think rural transit is always empty

reading.retellFrame: Sofia's subway ride and Eli's valley bus resemble each other in ___, but they differ in ___.
